utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam, and good afternoon to you too. The accused are here. If there are problems with interpretation, please let us know. Defence teams are here. There is Mr. Bourgon who is absent only, as far as see. Prosecution composition as yesterday, Mr. Nicholls, Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Thayer. Colonel, good afternoon. Welcome back. And we are grateful for your having managed to remain at our disposal this afternoon, which basically means that you've put us in a position to conclude your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We were halfway towards the end of the cross-examination by Madam Fauveau. Please go ahead. Needless to remind you, Colonel, you're still testifying pursuant to your solemn declaration which you don't need to repeat every time you enter the courtroom. So Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Colonel Koster, is it fair to say that when the refugees were in Potocari were able to have a shower?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the refugees had the opportunity to wash themselves on the compound. I'm not sure whether they were able to take a shower but they did have the opportunity to wash.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it also fair to say that the refugees were fed, were given something to eat?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: The refugees received food on the compound. Outside the compound the refugees did not receive food.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Isn't it fair to say that Serbs gave bread and water to the refugees?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: That's correct. But I thought you were asking about what they received from the DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: However, in spite of the food given by the DutchBat, in spite of the bread brought by the Serbs, can it be said that the food available was not enough for the refugees to stay there very long?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Can we therefore say that the refugees had to be transported somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: I'm not in a position to conclude that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At any rate, the refugees did not have their houses in Potocari, did they?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: The refugees came from the enclave in Srebrenica to Potocari. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: They couldn't therefore stay in Potocari, could they?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: I don't know that they couldn't stay in Potocari. It was not their original place of residence.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that no refugee said to you that they wanted to stay in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: I don't remember anybody telling me that at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yesterday, in -- on page 3096 in the French transcript, that when the refugees left, their personal belongings stayed along the road, on the road but also in the compound. Is it fair to say that the refugees left the compound on the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: As far as I remember, the majority of the refugees did indeed leave the compound on July 13.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you tell us when DutchBat left Potocari?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date at this time. I believe it was a week or a week and a half later.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Before they left Potocari, I'm thinking of DutchBat members, not of you personally, did you tidy up, did you clean up, as to the personal belongings left by the refugees?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly? Are you saying that I or one of my people cleared up their possessions? Because that's not the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: If it wasn't the case, the belongings the refugees had left in the compound, were they still in the compound when you left it?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Don't remember that. I indicated yesterday that I don't know who removed the items and whether they were still there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: However, during that week that you stayed in Potocari after most of the refugees had left, who else was there in the Potocari compound apart from you? Were there any other people in the compound?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: The members of the armed forces who were in the enclave at that time and were serving there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Were they then in the Potocari compound, within the compound?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: At any rate you don't know what happened to the personal belongings left by the refugees, do you?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: On the 25th of October, page 3027 of the French transcript, you said this: The bodies that we found were the bodies of people who had been shot in the back. I'd like to know this: Were you able to see how big the wound was -- how big the wounds were?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: How big were they? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that I thought that the wounded area was surrounded by blood and the injury looked like a bullet had entered there and the diameter of the wound including the blood was probably approximately two to three centimetres.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that these bodies had clothes on?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes. They were dressed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So you were able to see the damage on the clothing, not -- you didn't see the wounds themselves, did you?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: I could see the wound on some of the victims.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Does that mean that they were not clothed or did you remove their clothes?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: It was visible through the clothes. Apparently the clothes were slightly removed from the wound.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know the difference between a wound caused by an exit wound and the difference -- and the opposite, entry wound?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes. I know the difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you describe to us what an entry wound looks like?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: An entry wound is small in diameter and in any case smaller than an exit wound. Often exit wounds are rougher.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Were you close to the bodies, and when you were, if you were close to the bodies, did you look at the wounds from close-up?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: I didn't touch them. I examined the bodies while I was standing next to them, and that's how I examined the wounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: So how can you be sure that they were entry wounds?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: The wound appeared small, as far as the entrance opening was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could you tell us what the diameter was of the wounds?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: The wounds that I examined, I just described them. Wherever the wound was clearly visible, the diameter was roughly one centimetre.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You stated that the bodies were in a row. Were you able to determine whether the bodies had been moved once the people had been killed?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: I wasn't able to determine that, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: You also stated that you found documents next to the bodies. Yesterday you testified that you were not able to read them. I'd like to know this: Were you not able to understand what was on the paper or did you not recognise the handwriting or the script?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: No. It was because of the language in which they were written.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that when the refugees arrived in Potocari, they were mostly women, children and elderly people?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Do you know where the men went, the able-bodied men, or the military, from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Do you know where they went?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: No, I didn't know it at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that there was fighting between the Muslim military and the Serb military on the 12th of July, in the enclave -- 12th and the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: I received information about that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Fauveau. Mr. Krgovic? Mr. Krgovic is representing General Gvero here and he will be cross-examining you now. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel. I'll ask you some questions that have to do with the statement that you provided to the Prosecutor's Office, and this statement was provided on the 25th and 26th September 1995. My questions will be about an event that you described in that statement. Do you remember that towards the end of January 1995, Muslim fighters captured 100 members of the United Nations in the area called Bandera Trougao and they kept them hostage for a few days and they lived in very bad conditions during that time?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Only after the negotiations that Colonel Karremans conducted with Naser Oric were these people let go; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: No. I don't know what the course of the negotiations was or with whom they were conducted. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown Exhibit 1D44? Page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, this is in the third paragraph from the beginning and the sentence starts with, "[In English] That the negotiations were conducted with Naser Oric, the commander of the Muslim forces." [Interpretation] Did you find that?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes. I saw the passage, and I believe that I remembered it better at the time than I do now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. Could you please tell me whether, when these people were captured, the Muslim fighters did not leave them a possibility to go back to the base but, rather, kept them in custody until their final release? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: I don't understand the question. Would you please ask the question again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When these soldiers were kept on that day, the Muslim fighters would not let them go back to the base but, rather, kept them there? In other words, they didn't have a choice whether they could go back to the base once they entered that forbidden territory. That choice was not given to them. They could not opt for returning to the base. They were kept there.

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: As far as I remember, they were indeed held at that site.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, let me remind you of another detail that you mentioned in your statement. We are talking about one part of page 4 of this statement, the penultimate paragraph thereof. The beginning is, "[In English] Was provoked." "[Interpretation] Muslim fighters would take up the positions at the observation post at night and would fire in the direction of the Serbs. The Serb fighters would then respond by firing back." Do you remember these events and also do you remember having stated that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, you were in the Potocari base on the 11th of July because you mentioned that shells were falling around the base, in the vicinity of the base. You stated that yesterday in your testimony. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, when you were at the base, across the road from the Papa, did you have another observation point in the building with a machine-gun nest which was manned by your soldiers? Let me rephrase the question. I'm referring to the base itself. Was there an observation point in one of the buildings at the base which faced the observation point Papa, and if indeed there was an observation point in that building, was it manned by your soldiers, by UN soldiers?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was manned, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And from that point, one could see the surroundings of the base and the road leading northward?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: During that day, the 11th of July, did you spend any time at that place? Did you ever climb the stairs to go to the second floor of that building?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, if I were to tell you that a member of your unit testified before this Trial Chamber and said that on the 11th of July, he saw Muslim fighters in several groups opening fire from several mortars towards the Serb positions and then withdrawing, and that these mortar units were deployed around the base, to the left and to the right and to the north, would you accept that testimony as being accurate?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: I didn't see that personally so I can't accept that statement for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody report to you about that? Did you ever hear anything about that? Did you hear that the fact that fire had been opened resulted in the shelling of the positions of the Muslim fighters by the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Do you still mean on the 11th of June?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: July. Excuse me, the 11th of July. That morning, I saw -- I heard various reports about fighting that was taking place but I don't remember them in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, now I'm going to ask you something else that arises from your statement. I'm referring to page 6 -- I apologise, page 7, paragraph 3 from the bottom of the page. And the sentence starts with the following words. Page 7. "[English] The Serbian soldiers." "[Interpretation] The Serbian soldiers approached the post and told my fellow soldiers that they were coming to take the post. My fellow soldiers were given the choice of returning to the compound or of driving into the Serbian territory." Do you remember these events?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What you have stated here corresponds to the best of your recollection of the events?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, when you provided the statement, when you were debriefed on your return from Srebrenica, you stated that you were present during the negotiations between Major Franken and a Serbian Colonel. Amongst other things, they discussed the upcoming evacuation of the DutchBat and some other things. Can you remember that meeting?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes. I remember this meeting. At the time I was not seated at the table. I was basically the liaison between Mr. Franken, and the rest of the battalion did not want to be disturbed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that at that meeting, an agreement was reached on the evacuation of the wounded who had remained in the compound in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And these wounded men were handed over to the Red Cross on the 17th of July and on that day they left the base; is that correct? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: I know that people were handed over, but I don't remember the exact date any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: To the Red Cross? This is what you stated in your statement. I'm just reminding you of that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes. I do remember it happening that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Colonel, let me take you back to a question that was put to you by my learned colleague Fauveau who asked you about separation. Was there a case in Potocari that women were separated from other women, that a woman was not allowed to get on a bus? Were there such cases?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: One more topic and I'm drawing to an end of my cross-examination. As far as I could understand you, you were a logistics officer. Did I understand your testimony well?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: During the deployment as it was proceeding normally, that was true, and afterwards I received additional duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the period before the conflict broke out in Srebrenica, so I'm talking about the period from the time that you arrived to early June 1995.

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: That's correct. At that time, I was indeed active as the logistics officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And as such, you knew about the quantity of fuel that the DutchBat had at its disposal and what the requirements were for fuel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In that period that I just mentioned, did you ever receive a request from your immediate superior or from the army of Republika Srpska what the monthly requirements or the monthly expenditures of fuel were of DutchBat?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: No. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if any of your subordinates or superiors provided such information to the command or the army of Republika Srpska at their request?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that with the last fuel delivery to DutchBat, a certain amount of that fuel was given to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that there was a protest from the Serb side because of that?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Would you please repeat who delivered the fuel to whom? That was confusing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The last fuel delivery received by DutchBat, a certain quantity from that contingent was provided to the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Are you asking me whether I know about that or are you asking me who did that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes? Mr. Haynes is representing Colonel Pandurevic or General Pandurevic. Perhaps before Mr. Haynes starts with his questions, perhaps there was one further question, it was a compound question basically, but one part of it has remained unanswered. One question was whether you heard, whether you at any time became aware that part of the final consignment ended up or was provided to the BiH army. The other one related to a formal complaint which supposedly was made by the Serbian, Bosnian Serb authorities. Are you aware of any such complaint ever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Colonel. Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Koster, in 1995, you were a Lieutenant in the 13th Airborne Battalion, that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: The 13th Battalion, that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that was an infantry battalion?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: That's correct. I was an infantryman myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, you've answered my next question. You were, as you've told Mr. Krgovic, the commander in charge of logistics. Was that a position you held at the base at Assen or was it one that you assumed after arriving in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: No. I also had that position in Assen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In 1995, you were 26 years of age. You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And in Srebrenica, your immediate superior was Colonel Franken, the deputy commanding officer for the battalion?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Prior to your tour of duty in Srebrenica, had you ever had any combat or wartime experience?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: No. I had not previously been in a war situation. Only in exercises.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And would that have been true of many of, if not all of, the men under your command?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: That would be true for the majority. Some of them served in Lebanon and experienced fighting there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as logistics officer, would you agree that you were responsible for ensuring that the battalion had everything it needed to function efficiently?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Certainly. Would you agree that the logistics officer is responsible for ensuring that the battalion has everything it needs to function efficiently?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that includes food, transport, clothing, weaponry, and fuel?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes. Those are things that are necessary for the battalion to function.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And would you agree that during your tour of duty in Srebrenica, it was your view as logistics officer that the morale of the battalion was good?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Well, that varied from the point when people had to subsist for longer periods of time on combat rations, their morale would diminish, but -- and then there was the rejection of leave convoys. That also dampened the mood, although it was still possible to function.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, your base as logistics officer was at Potocari, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you have an office there?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: We shared an office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And in the office that you shared, were records kept, for example, of the receipt of fuel and its disbursement?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And were those records that comprised both documents and computer files?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes. We used computers there, and we used paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, as commander of logistics, were you responsible for the maintenance of those records?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Very generally yes. I didn't do it personally. My people did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What, people under your command?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: People who were part of my logistics division, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, on the 11th of July, you went to Potocari. Did you go to the office that you shared?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: When the shelling and the fighting started, I did indeed return to the office I shared to draft a clearance request. I did that together with Major Franken during the shelling, but I don't remember whether that was the 10th or the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, whatever day it was, were the computers still intact and the paper records still intact?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Some of the papers had been taken to the bunkers but the ones that I needed to amend the request, that's what needed to be done at that point, and to print it out, those were available. I was able to amend the request there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How many Dutch soldiers, in your estimation, were present at Potocari during the 11th and 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: I'd have to give you a very rough estimate. I estimate that there were about 150 or 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how many refugees, in your rough estimate, did they have to deal with during those two days?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Which two days?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The 11th and 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Well, my rough estimate is that on the compound there were about 4.000 to 5.000 people. Outside the compound, there were far more. So on the -- if there are 4.000 to 5.000 people on the compound, they were being helped by my men and there were several people outside the compound as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, all your logistics records were destroyed, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: I know that most of the documents and records were destroyed. I don't know whether everything was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was that on your order?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: No, because when those orders arrived, I was active outside the compound as commander for the reception of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you know whose order it was to destroy those documents?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: That would have been either Major Franken or Lieutenant Colonel Karremans.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And do you know when the order was given and when it was executed?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: I don't know when the order was issued. I know it was executed when it became clear that the Serb military intended to enter the compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you really not help us with the date?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: It must have been the day that the Bosnian Serb military arrived. And that would have been on the 12th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you help us as to why it was so important that fuel disbursement records, for example, were destroyed at that moment in time?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Those data were part of operational information, and we didn't want those to fall into the hands of the adversary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Is that correct? Or is there not a distinction between logistics information and operational information?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: The distinction exists but there is an overlap when we are dealing with information about weapons and ammunition which are also logistics data. If I surrender those then it also reveals something about my operations and you don't want to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to move on. Your second sphere of responsibility was as commander of the battalion reserve. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes. I did that temporarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Help me. On my reading of your debriefing document, the battalion reserve was created in about late May or early June of 1995. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: I think that's about right. I'd have to reread my statement to see what the exact date was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's probably not important, but it was about that time, and under your command would have been, for example, Captain Groen?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was it he who succeeded you when you ceased to be commander of the battalion reserve on the 11th of July?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: No. Captain Groen was the commander of Bravo Company, and I was succeeded by somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Anyway, as commander of the battalion reserve during June of 1995, were you deployed on a number of occasions to the south of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And was the purpose of that so that you could familiarise yourself with the terrain there?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a section of video now, if I may, because I imagine it's some little while since you've seen the south of Srebrenica. This is P01514. It's the Ruez trial video, south to Srebrenica. Would you watch it then I'm going to ask you a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just two questions. I hope that reminded you of the terrain to the south of Srebrenica. Did it?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: No. That's the first time I've seen a helicopter view.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, would you agree with me that access and egress to and from the south of Srebrenica by vehicle can only be achieved by road?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: From which direction do you mean? Do you mean from the enclave or from outside the enclave?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I mean from outside the enclave, getting into Srebrenica from the south. The only way to get there in a vehicle is by road?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: It depends on how you want to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, did you take your APCs across those hills we've just seen in that helicopter shot or did you stay on the road with them?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: I stayed on the road in my APC.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you see any feasible possibility to travel across country in your APC or was travelling on the road the only feasible possibility?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: If you are referring to the roads, I would prefer to stay on the road. That's in armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The second question I want to ask you about the terrain to the south of the enclave is about fields of vision. Your fields of vision in the south of the enclave are extremely limited by the mountainous terrain, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to move on. When you were deployed to the south of the enclave, did you ever come across Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you ever encounter Muslim forces that were wearing Ukrainian army uniforms?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: I wouldn't recognise the uniforms as such so I can't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of Muslim forces who were equipped with Ukrainian army uniforms?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Then I shall ask you no further questions. Thank you very much, Mr. Koster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Haynes. Is there re-examination, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So before you start with your cross-examination - your re-examination, sorry - can I just draw your attention that you need to put -- since one of his statements was admitted or has been admitted recently, after the amendments under the Rule 92 ter, then one of the requirements so that that admittance becomes final is that the witness attests that the written statement or transcript accurately reflects the witness's declaration and what he would say if examined. When you started with the witness, not yesterday, the previous day, you did refer him to your -- to the correctness of your summary but not exactly to the correctness of his previous Rule 61 proceedings statement. So you need to do that, please. You don't need to do it in relation to what had already previously been admitted under Rule 92 bis before the amendments, the paragraph (C), Rule 92 bis(C) came into existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll start there, Your Honour. I can take care of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I would suggest in future whenever you -- we are dealing with Rule 92 ter evidence, after reading the summary, you don't only ask the witness in relation -- questions in relation to the summary but also in relation to the testimony so that we stick to the letter of the law and not only to the spirit of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We will make that our practice, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Colonel Koster. When we met in preparation of your testimony, were you given an opportunity to review the written transcript of the testimony that you gave in the Mladic and Karadzic preliminary proceedings?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you in fact review each and every page of the transcript, that written transcript, of those proceedings, sir?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you attest to the accuracy of the contents of that transcript as being faithful to the testimony that you gave at that time, sir?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Will that suffice, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'd just like to take up a couple quick questions with you, Colonel Koster. You testified that there were no fuel deliveries between mid-February and June.

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you make any requests for fuel through your chain of command and then ultimately the VRS during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: Absolutely. On every logistics convoy that was requested, the quantity of fuel that we desired to receive was always indicated, and it was also always refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention to a question that my learned colleague, Mr. Lazarevic, asked you yesterday at page 50, beginning at line 22, and I just want to clarify something for the record because he asked you a question and I don't think you answered the second part of it and I just want to ask you that directly again. He asked you, "Besides the fact that warrant officer van Schaik did not compare the ID documents with the persons whom you found there, and this wasn't done by yourself or by your colleague Rutten either; is that correct?" Can you tell the Trial Chamber whether to your knowledge Lieutenant Rutten ever tried to compare whatever documents were there with the bodies?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: No. I apologise, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, I think I put a question to the witness myself yesterday, asking whether any of those witnesses contained any photos. And he said that no, they contained text, and text in a language that he could not read or understand. How can you compare a document containing text only with a dead body or -- I don't know. I mean, what's the purpose of your --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Your Honour. He answered the question as to himself. The question was put to him. I just didn't want to leave an unanswered question out there. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Colonel, you were asked yesterday, at page 67 of the trial transcript, regarding the leave that you took in April of 1995. Do you recall what you told the Office of the Prosecutor in September of 1995 with respect to the date of the last convoy of DutchBat soldiers which was permitted to return to the enclave after taking leave?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: As best I can remember, I indicated that the convoy was indeed the last convoy of people on leave that returned, and I was on that convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Colonel, turning your attention to page 70 of yesterday's testimony, you were also asked by my learned colleague, Madam Fauveau, whether you were not supposed to let the refugees into the compound when they first began arriving on 11 July. And you answered that that is correct. Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: That's correct. I did not receive authorisation from the battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you know why that authorisation was not given to you at that time, sir?

utterances.speaker: EELCO CHRISTIAN MARTIN JODOCUS KOSTER
utterances.text: I was told that the authorisation was not yet being given because Bosnian Serb forces had threatened to shell the compound, and that's why it was unwise to admit the refugees to the compound, to avoid the risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Colonel. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Thayer. Colonel, we've finished with your testimony now. I wish to thank you on behalf of the Trial Chamber, on behalf of Judge Kwon, Judge Prost, and Judge Stole for having come over to give testimony, to give evidence in this case. You will be assisted by our staff to organise your return. I suppose you're not going too far but in any case we wish you a safe journey to wherever you're going. Thank you for coming over.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, shall we dispose of the issue that was raised yesterday by Madam Fauveau and then have the break immediately after? Yes. But before, we need to finalise the exhibit issue. Yesterday, you tendered -- I don't have the list here now -- are there any further -- Madam Fauveau, none? No more. Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's always that difficult question as to whether you admit as a separate exhibit a small piece of film that's already gone in, in its entirety. I take the view that it's unnecessary. I was explicit in the question that it was Exhibit P01514 and southbound to Srebrenica. So I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree entirely with you and the rest of the Bench does.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you, Mr. Haynes. Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I was just standing up to move, Your Honour. I can respond to any other exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. We'll soon have a new witness come into this courtroom who enjoys some protective measures. We are not going to deal with those. We are handing down a -- our oral decision on an oral motion tabled yesterday during yesterday's sitting, towards the end, by Madam Fauveau appearing for General Miletic. Madam Fauveau requested that the cross-examination of the next witness, namely Witness Number 25, who, as I said, is due to start giving testimony within minutes, should be unrestricted and not limited to the issue of nine bodies found in Potocari, as decided by us in paragraph 67 of our 12th September decision. We have received submissions, oral submissions, from Madam Fauveau, from Mr. Josse, orally from Mr. Nicholls yesterday, but the Prosecution followed with a formal response filed today, and I must point out to you, Mr. Nicholls, that you failed to indicate on the front page the name of Mr. David Josse, who was appearing together with Mr. Krgovic for General Gvero. Try to avoid that in the future. We start by making it clear that the restriction of the cross-examination of Witness 25 that I referred to earlier on was not removed by our decision of the -- by our decision on the Defence motion for certification, which we handed down on the 19th of October. In the Prosecution's submission, later on, they sought to admit the transcript of Witness 25 pursuant also to Rule 92 ter and in the alternative pursuant to Rule 89(F). You will recall that following our decision in relation to the previous ordered redaction, in the statement of this witness, we had pointed out that basically the Prosecution's request to tender again the document under Rule 92 ter was basically superseded, unnecessary, redundant, and to our recollection, this was acknowledged as being so by Mr. McCloskey here in the courtroom. I don't need to recall verbatim or read out the various amendments that were introduced recently to the rules, and pursuant to which we have not only paragraph 92 bis(C) but also 92 ter. I will just point out on behalf of the Trial Chamber that the main change introduced by these amendments to the procedure, when a 92 bis witness is required to appear for cross-examination, is, provided that that decision is taken after the amendments came into force, is that that witness would be required to attest that his or her written statement or transcript accurately reflects his or her declaration or what he or she would say if examined again. Basically, the Rules, both before and after the amendments of the 13th September 2006, do not address the position where the Trial Chamber decides to require the witness to appear for cross-examination in respect of part of his or her transcript which would be admitted under Rule 92 bis. However, the practice existed and it was acknowledged also jurisprudentially here, that the correct interpretation of former Rule 92 bis(E) permitted, allowed, the Trial Chamber to restrict cross-examination to only a part of the previous transcript or statement when this was deemed appropriate. It is our firm belief that this has not changed now by the introduction of either 92 bis(C) or 92 ter. The power that existed with the Trial Chamber, with any Trial Chamber to restrict cross-examination existed before and continues to exist. In other words, we read current Rule 92 bis(C) as meaning that Trial Chambers are still permitted the same -- to limit cross-examination. If this is so, we believe it cannot be otherwise, then the reference to the applicability of Rule 92 ter can only apply to that part of the written statement or transcript in respect of which the witness is to be cross-examined, and would not extend to the rest of the testimony, transcript or statement on which there would be no cross-examination. Our conclusion, therefore, is that Rule 92 ter plainly does not apply to a written statement or transcript admitted under Rule 92 bis if the witness is not required to appear for cross-examination. Therefore, the provisions of Rule 92 ter ought not to apply to that part of the written statement or transcript admitted under Rule 92 bis in respect of which the witness is not to be cross-examined. Basically, the conclusion is, our decision is, therefore, that your contention, your request, Madam Fauveau, that the introduction of Rule 92 ter requires or calls for the full cross-examination of Rule 92 bis witnesses can only be rejected. In addition to this, we also wish to state that, although there still is on record, in one of the submissions of the Prosecution, the request to tender this statement under Rule 92 ter, the position is that that has not been decided and we see absolutely no need for it to be decided, especially after having heard what Mr. McCloskey stated in one of the previous sittings. Therefore, the decision is as follows: The witness will -- the cross-examination that we ordered previously, and which we specifically limited, as I stated earlier on, stands, and your request to have it -- to have cross-examination extended to other issues is hereby rejected. Yes. I noticed you wished to state something.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would just like to specify that my request did not relate to 92 bis witnesses. I fully agree that the Trial Chamber still has the power to limit and restrict the cross-examination of 92 bis witnesses. My request only related to the admission of 92 ter witnesses. Of course, if the witness is not admitted pursuant to 92 ter, then my request is dropped. But I never said that you had no power to restrict the cross-examination pursuant to 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I understood your motion yesterday to specifically mean Prosecution has asked -- was not satisfied with having had this statement [French interpretation coming over English channel]. Okay. We don't need translation into French.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry. [French interpretation coming over English channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci. Yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I take that as I should probably just sit down but just on a related, and in fact if I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can stay where you are. We can see you, at least if not completely, I mean we ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just on a related topic that might be helpful now that -- just for some food for thought, is that you may know we are now -- we are coming up next week to some 89(F) witnesses or now 92 ter witnesses. I've realised that we have not asked leave for court to go into that. I'm not sure you would require us to or not. And with all the filings that we have to do and that we are reading, I would propose that we can perhaps deal with these subjects orally because, unlike 92 bis, these 89(F)/92 ter requests are -- basically we have one reason that we are offering them and that is just to help save time, and I've asked Defence counsel to consider these witnesses, that they have been on notice for, you know, months and months now, because we listed the rule next to their name, whether they had any objections or they are thinking about that. It's the next -- well, the -- the next -- next week are the first three witnesses. So I would just offer that to you for thought, and we are, of course, ready to do whatever you feel is appropriate. But basically our submission is all the same. We would just like to save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will come back to you on this soon after the break. We'll have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One thing, because obviously we don't come out with our decisions without having discussed the merits fully, the understanding also is, pursuant to what we decided a few minutes ago, that if Mr. Nicholls in this case, after reading the summary to the witness, puts questions in chief on other matters, on whatever matter basically, this could entitle you, of course, to cross-examine the witness on that matter. In other words, the restricted cross-examination would immediately extend to these new issues that would be then with the witness. Okay? So, we'll have a 25-minute break. We also need to finish at quarter to 7.00 this evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would just say, sorry, Your Honours, the witness is not available, he's told me, Monday or Tuesday, so I would strongly hope we can finish him today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Very soon you're going to start giving evidence here which will be almost entirely cross-examination and limited also to one particular area which will soon be mentioned to you. Our rules require that before you start your testimony, you enter a solemn declaration to the effect that in the course of your testimony, you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Madam Usher is going to hand to you the text of this solemn declaration. Please read it out loud and that will be your undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me explain a few things briefly before you start giving evidence. The Prosecution requested on your behalf and we granted the Prosecution's request that you will enjoy some protective measures in this trial, while you give evidence. One protective measure that we have granted is to hide your identity. You will not be referred to by your first name or by your family name, but you will be referred to by a pseudonym, which in your case is PW -- that's Prosecution Witness -- 114. Of course, lawyers can address you sir or witness, et cetera, but please refrain from ever making reference to the witness's name and surname. The other thing, again in our effort to hide your identity, is that we have granted facial distortion. Basically that means that outside this room where you are testifying, and of course behind these glasses where we have some staff translating and assisting the Trial Chamber, no one will be able to see your face. That is the second protective measure that we have granted. Very soon, if you will have your -- if you look at your screen on your monitor, very soon you will see how you will appear to others. In other words, in squares like you're seeing now. Is that to your satisfaction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So Mr. Nicholls will now read you out a brief summary, maybe ask you some questions, I don't know, and then he would be immediately followed by the Defence teams on cross-examination. I'll tell you when we come to the cross-examination what the restriction imposed by this Trial Chamber is, namely they can't cross-examine you on everything unless we change our decision but only on some things that you allegedly saw only with reference to some dead bodies that you saw in Potocari, allegedly. Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First in e-court could we have P02270 which is the pseudonym sheet? And that should not be broadcast, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. I think it would be simpler in this case if we use the usual system, you show the witness a sheet of paper with his name and surname and then it will be saved under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, could you please look at that sheet of paper, do not read it out loud, but can you confirm that your name is printed on the piece of paper under PW 114?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-114
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam could you kindly show it to the Defence teams? Do you want to see it all or is it enough if, say, Mr. Ostojic or Mr. Meek sees it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sure it's enough for my learned friends to see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's enough. Could we see it, please? Okay. That's yours. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I apologise to the witness. I have two small housekeeping matters before I ask the witness questions. The first, and I've talked about this with counsel on the other side, I noticed that in the prior testimony, in the Krstic transcript, there was another reference to a commander Nikolic which was not part of the Court's decision and had not been listed. That is at page 1569, line 25. I will affirm that as with all other references to the transcript, that is to Momir Nikolic. It was in a question from the Bench that the name appears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you satisfied with that, Madam Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. We don't need to take any provisions on that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to raise it because I noticed it when I read it. The second issue is that P02189 in e-court, that is Exhibit P52A from this witness's prior testimony, the wrong image is stored. And we are correcting that. It's a technical problem. It has been corrected. I'm sorry, I didn't realise that it had been corrected while we are waiting today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Were you all made aware of this, Defence teams?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I had not told my colleagues that. I had hard copies of the exhibit in case any of them wanted to use it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When we come to that if there are problems please let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, I'm now going to read a brief summary of your prior testimony and if I make any mistakes, please correct me at the end. On 12 July, Witness 114 and another DutchBat soldier went to investigate rumours of corpses in the vicinity of the DutchBat base in Potocari. In an area behind the "White House," some 700 metres from the UN compound, the witness saw nine or ten corpses. The witness marked the location of the bodies, a stream, and the "White House" on Krstic Exhibit 5/3 A.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that is P02190 in this case. The bodies lay approximately 20 metres from the witness down a hill and near a stream. The bodies lay in a line on the edge of a forest. Using his colleague's camera, witness 114 took three photos of the bodies. And those are Exhibits P02191, P02192 and P02193. The witness's colleague stood on guard while the witness took these photos because there were many Serb soldiers, Rambo-types, in the vicinity at the time. The bodies were dressed in civilian clothes, blue jeans, pullovers, coats. None of the victims wore military clothing. All of the victims were men, the age group was 15 to 45. The witness could see that some of the victims had blood stains on their backs and on the backs of their heads. After seeing these victims, and taking the three photographs of the nine to ten bodies, the witness and the other DutchBat soldier immediately returned to the UN compound. This was around noon on 12 July.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, when we met earlier, you reviewed your transcript from the Krstic trial; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-114
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Is what I've just read an accurate summary of your testimony in that trial?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-114
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I now have a question for you. You testified as I stated in the summary that the bodies were lying in a line. Can you tell the Trial Chamber, please, the position of the bodies, how they were lying as they lay in that line?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-114
utterances.text: The bodies why lying in a line with the head down in the stream on the stomach so they were shot from the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you Mr. Nicholls. Who is going first? Ms. Condon? Let's make an effort to finish with this witness today.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Witness, I want to ask you about the date that you say that you found the bodies. Your evidence to this Trial Chamber is that it's the 12th of July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-114
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And you're sure about that date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-114
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Can I ask you what time of the day it was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-114
utterances.text: Approximately noon.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: About noon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-114
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: And you took some photos of what you say you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-114
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Yeah. It stands to reason, doesn't it, that the photos were taken on the same day as you made the discovery?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-114
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between question and answer? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. You're both speaking the same language so try to pause between question and answer, both of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Now, witness, you recall being interviewed by the Royal Dutch police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-114
utterances.text: In the beginning, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Perhaps, Your Honour, if the witness could be shown 1D48, at page 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think that may be something that needs to be under seal or not broadcast to the gallery because the witness is protected.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. Perhaps if we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're 100 per cent right, Mr. Nicholls. Has it been broadcast? No? All right. Okay. Shall we go straight into private session? I think it's easier if we go into private session and deal with it like that. I think the safest way is to deal with it in private session because then there will definitely be no broadcast. I can't guarantee if we are not in private session. So let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ostojic is representing Colonel Beara in this case and will be asking you some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir, how are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-114
utterances.text: I'm fine, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just have a couple of questions for you. You mention on page 35, line 20, I believe, or during the statement "Rambo-type." Can you describe for me in greater detail what you mean whether you say Rambo-type soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-114
utterances.text: I think it were like some soldier reserves, reserves units, and soldiers who are not on active duty at that time, just some of them on stand-by or call. They were wearing normal civilian clothes and half military clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Soldiers that were perhaps not within the regular army or the Drina Corps as you've identified them previously in your testimony, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-114
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And in fact, sir, am I correct that you've called these Rambo-type soldiers temps or temporary soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-114
utterances.text: Yes, temporary soldiers who are on call, like a reserve units.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you distinguish between the temporary or Rambo-type soldiers from the others soldiers because of what factors?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-114
utterances.text: The -- it was a free-phase. The first phase was in a very organised unit, an infantry unit, was on strict control of a commander. The second way was the Rambo types, they were on -- they were on an -- a command, they had a commander but not a strict command. So they were doing their own thing, entering houses, taking stuff, and walking around without, you know, so there was the second way.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And is it true sir that these Rambo-type soldiers are the soldiers that you believe committed violation of human rights?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-114
utterances.text: I think that's possible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, isn't that something that you testified to in the Krstic case, under oath, and you didn't state there that it was possible. You, in fact, sir, made it an affirmative fact that it was your opinion that the it was the Rambo-type soldiers not the regular soldiers who committed those war crimes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-114
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I have a transcript reference, please, since it's -- specific wording is being put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the Trial Chamber would need to see that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll give it to you but I think the witness answered the question. Specifically the 29th of March 2000, page 1562, lines 1 through 13 in complete context.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And in fact sir these regular Serb soldiers, the disciplined ones, it was your opinion at that time, and perhaps today, that they didn't have time for that because they had other duties, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-114
utterances.text: Yeah, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have to ask you this question and I just want to make sure the Court is aware because of the Court's ruling I'm not sure if I can ask you this: Can you tell me the date that you saw Mr. Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: First of all, the question put about the Rambo-type soldiers is -- does not accurately reflect what's in the transcript. The witness never said it was a Rambo-type soldiers not other soldiers who committed violations of human rights. Second, I've been pretty patient but I'm waiting for him to tie this into the area of cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Cross-examination, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But just for the record, the basis put is not reflected in the transcript and my friend's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you wish to argue this, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Wholeheartedly I could argue it, Your Honour. If you look on page 35, line 20 of Mr. Nicholls' summary, he mentions the word Rambo-type and I'm flushing that out and I think in the statement that is given I could read it to the witness but I think this witness gave us his honest opinion and answered my question having his recollection and he answered it the way he felt and I think he answered it honestly. If the Court wants, I could read either that portion of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But what the Court wants is that you go straight to the questions that pertain to the limited or restricted cross-examination issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I appreciate that, Your Honour, but we could discuss it perhaps outside the witness's -- the Court said if they go beyond that and mention things like Rambo-type which they mentioned the door should be opened, so I asked him that question given the Court's ruling. Fair enough?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I said Mr. Ostojic is if questions are put to the witness on other issues on other matters, beyond or apart from the restricted issues reserved for cross-examinations then you will be allowed to but the witness was not asked questions about these Rambo-types. I allow -- we allowed you to put one or two questions on these Rambo, at least to clear but now go straight to the issue that the cross-examination has been restricted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, thank you for your patience, given your testimony here today and given your testimony in Krstic approximately six and a half years ago, would I be fair to suggest to you that in fact the murders that were committed of those nine individuals, that you found on the 12th of July, were committed indeed by these Rambo, rogue type soldiers or people? Isn't that accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-114
utterances.text: It's true, yeah, I think it's possible, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you. Madam Nikolic, are you going to cross examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't have any questions for this witness, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. With your permission, I would have a couple of questions about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Mr. Stojanovic is appearing for Borovcanin, for Accused Borovcanin in this case. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to show you a video clip of the area that we will be using and I will kindly ask you to assist me with it and I would like to use 01516. This is the aerial clip that I'm showing. Could we please bring that up on e-court? While this is happening, I would kindly ask you to answer a few questions. The road that you took to the place where you found the bodies, was that an asphalt road, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-114
utterances.text: No that was not an asphalt road. This was a gravel road.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you say that part of the road was asphalt and the other part was gravel or was it all gravel? What would you say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-114
utterances.text: Maybe the -- maybe the first 25 metres was a bit of asphalt and then the half, the next was up in the mountains was a normal gravel, mud, muddy road, normally in the winter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Had you ever used that road before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-114
utterances.text: Yes. Many times we did a patrol, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that it was a customary route when you went on patrols?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-114
utterances.text: Yes. It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did the road go by the houses or did it lead through a non-inhabited area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-114
utterances.text: There were a couple of houses and then it was in the middle of no where, in the forest mostly, and then up to the hills were green grass fields, that's all, and some bunkers, Muslim bunkers. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How did you learn about a certain number of bodies there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-114
utterances.text: The day on the 12th it was a rumour going around on -- it was already on the 11th there was a rumour around on the compound about bodies and on the 12th I went walking around and I found the bodies. So it was a rumour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that on the second day of the evacuation of the population that you set off in your mission to find the bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-114
utterances.text: Yes, on the second day, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: On the second day of the evacuation you went to see where those bodies were, would that be the precise answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think this has been covered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are right. Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will continue, Your Honour. I believe that we have to clarify some things.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did somebody tell you directly to go and see those bodies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Clarifying is one thing and repeating is another. Please try not to repeat the same questions that others or which are not in doubt in any case. Yes. Go ahead with your question. The question to you is, sir, whether anyone gave you instructions to go where the bodies were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was in my own will. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: How long did it take you to get to those bodies when you were walking on that macadam road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-114
utterances.text: A couple of minutes. It's not far from the compound. I was working around the compound the main entrance where they -- transport of the Muslim people were heading to the buses. I was working there so maybe five, six minutes. It's not far, 700 metres, approx.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And now I would kindly ask the usher to assist us and I would like to ask the witness to look at the aerial image in front of him. Could you try and mark the route that you took to the bodies? If you need time to get your bearings and see where certain facilities are on this image that shouldn't be a problem. We have time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If the witness wishes, it can be blown up. I don't know if he knows that can be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: First I would zoom out so that he gets a complete picture of the aerial image that we have at our disposal and then he can indicate where he would like the technicians to zoom in and we can proceed from there. Let's zoom out first, please. And get the complete picture on the screen, complete image. Yes. Witness, we are giving you the opportunity to look at this image and then in relation to any question that may be put to you, to ask or indicate to us where you would like the technicians to zoom in and then you can mark whatever has been asked from you, mainly the route you took.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was standing here on this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went up here and then through this tree line here, this is a muddy way, and up here, this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Can you finish it with an X, please, with the letter X?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And to the right of it, could you kindly put your signature and date? Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Or perhaps 114 as his pseudonym or we keep it under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. PW-114.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You could cancel that and put 114. That's what we require. PW -- PW-114. I thank you. Yes Mr. Stojanovic?
